title: Scotch Woodcock
subtitle: Scrambled eggs on buttered toast with anchovy paste
excerpt: Soft scrambled eggs on buttered toast spread with anchovy paste, finished with a little cream and seasoned generously. A Victorian savoury that delivers far more flavour than it has any right to.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. Scotch woodcock listed under savouries, as a course served after the sweet at formal dinners. The name refers to the appearance of anchovy paste on egg, said to resemble the woodcock bird, no actual woodcock is involved. Also found in Eliza Acton, Modern Cookery for Private Families (1845).

content.text: Scotch woodcock is soft scrambled eggs on toast spread with anchovy paste. The name is a Victorian joke: there is no woodcock in it. What it is, in practice, is one of the best quick breakfasts or savouries in British cooking. The anchovy base adds a deep, savoury flavour that makes the eggs taste considerably more complex than they are. It takes 10 minutes.

items.prepNote: or 4 anchovy fillets mashed to a paste

content.text: Toast {{bread-white}} bread slices and butter immediately with {{salted-butter}} of salted butter. Spread the {{anchovy-paste}} of anchovy paste thinly but evenly over the buttered toast. Keep warm.
Beat {{eggs}} eggs with {{double-cream}} of double cream and a good grinding of black pepper. No salt: the anchovy provides it.

Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a small saucepan over very low heat. Add the egg mixture and stir slowly and constantly with a wooden spoon or rubber spatula, scraping the base of the pan. The eggs should take 4 to 5 minutes to set to a soft, creamy curd. Pull off the heat while still slightly underdone: they will continue cooking from the residual heat of the pan.
Spoon the scrambled eggs onto the anchovy toast. Scatter over snipped chives if using. Serve immediately.

rows.cause: Cooked too fast over high heat
rows.fix: Scrambled eggs for Scotch woodcock need very low heat and constant movement. They should take at least 4 minutes.

rows.cause: Salt added to the eggs as well as the anchovy paste
rows.fix: Do not season the eggs with salt. The anchovy paste and the salty butter on the toast provide all the salt needed.

rows.cause: Applied too thickly or a very salty brand used
rows.fix: Use a thin, even spread. Gentleman's Relish (Patum Peperium) is traditional and well-balanced; other pastes vary considerably in intensity.

rows.symptom: Eggs set before the toast is ready
rows.cause: Started cooking the eggs before the toast was done
rows.fix: Get the toast, butter, and anchovy paste ready and plated before starting the eggs. The eggs take about 5 minutes; the toast should already be done.

content.text: Scotch woodcock was a savoury course at Victorian and Edwardian dinner parties. It came after the pudding as a sharp finish before the port. The anchovy-on-egg combination earned it the whimsical name of a game bird. It fell from formal menus in the mid-twentieth century. It survives as a breakfast or late-night supper dish, especially in households that keep anchovy paste.
